1.

By this award, claim petition under section 166 & 140 of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, would be
decided.
2.  The facts as stated in the claim petition are as under:-

Deceased Kosar, Mother of Petitioner No.1 to Petitioner No.9, died on account of a motor accident which happened on 09.01.2018 at about 05:30 a.m., near Dhaba at Jaisinghpur Khera, NH-8, Rewari, PS-Bawal, Rewari, Haryana.

In connection with this accident, an FIR No.06/2018, u/s 279/304-A IPC, was registered at PS Bawal,
Rewari, Haryana on 09.01.2018.

As per the claim petition, at the relevant time,
Petitioner No.1 was coming back from Ajmer to Delhi by bus with his mother namely Kosar and when they reached at Jasinghpur Khera, NH-8, Rewari (HR), the driver of the bus stopped bus at a Dhaba for breakfast.

Deceased was standing on footpath at Dhaba side, when all of a sudden, the offending vehicle bearing Registration No. HR-38S-4053 (Hayva) came from behind of the deceased in very high speed and hit her from backside and due to this powerful impact deceased fell down on road side and died on the spot.
3. On service of notice of the petition, all the three respondents marked appearance and filed their written statements.

Respondent No.1 & Respondent No.2 filed joint written statement mentioning that the accident did not take place due to negligence of R1 and that the deceased was hit by an unknown vehicle and after hitting, the unknown vehicle fled away from the spot.
It is further submitted that the alleged offending vehicle is duly insured with R3/IFFCO Tokio GIC Ltd. & R1 was having valid driving licence at the time of accident.

The insurance company/ Respondent No.3 has filed its written statement separately and it is specifically stated in the written statement that the petitioners are not the legal heirs and not dependents of the alleged deceased.

It is further submitted that no accident involving insured vehicle has ever taken place and same has been falsely implicated Abdul Kalam Etc vs Hamid Etc on 9 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/46110034/
2 later on, so as to extract compensation.

sentences.text: It is further submitted that driver of the alleged offending vehicle was not holding a valid and effective driving licence at the relevant time and the said vehicle was being plied without a valid permit at the relevant time.
Other general defences have been taken by R3/Insurer.

4. On the basis of pleadings, following issues were framed on 28.08.2018 :-
(i) Whether Smt. Kosar died in a motor vehicular accident, which happened on 09.01.2018 at about 5:30 a.m. near Dhaba at Jaisinghpur Khera, NH-18, Rewari,
Haryana, within the jurisdiction of PS Bawal, Rewari due to rash and negligent driving of motor vehicle bearing Registration No. HR-38S-4053 (Dumper) (Hayva)
by the Respondent No. 1 / Hamid?

(OPP) 
(ii) Whether the Respondent No.1 was holding a valid driving licence to drive the said dumper and the said dumper was used on the public road on a valid permit, if not, its effect?
(OPR3)
(iii) Whether the petitioners are entitled to compensation,if so, to what amount and from whom?

(OPP) 
(iv) Whether the petitioners are entitled to interest on the award amount, if so, at what rate of interest and for which period?
(v) Relief 5.

Petitioner side examined only one witness i.e. Petitioner No.1.
5(i).

Petitioner No.1 Sh. Abdul Kalam (PW1), himself stepped into the witness box and relied upon affidavit Ex.PW1/A & Ex.PW1/B and deposed about the manner of accident and relied upon the following documents:
(i) Copy of Voter I.D. Card and Aadhar Cards of Petitioner (ii) Certified copy of criminal case record is Ex.PW1/2 (iii) Copy of Aadhar Card of deceased Kausar Begam is Ex.PW1/3.
PW1 has been further examined as an eye-witness to the accident and deposed regarding manner of accident.

Thereafter, PE was closed.
6.
Respondent have opted not to examine any witness in their defence.

I have heard Sh. G.M. Rajesh, counsel for petitioners and Sh. Akshay Kumar, Ld. Counsel for R3/
insurer.
Record of the case has also been perused.
8. In an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and in fact, is the preponderance of probabilities which is applied in civil cases.
It is also the law that the tribunal is not bound by the technical rules of evidence.
Further, in holding any inquiry under section 168, The Claims Tribunal may follow such summary procedure as it thinks fit.
9. In order to prove the case, petitioner examined one witness i.e. P1 as eye-witness namely Abdul Kalam.

PW1 testified that on 09.01.2018 he alongwith his mother were travelling in a bus from Ajmer to Delhi and at about 05:30 a.m., when the bus reached at Jaisinghpur, Khera, NH-8, Rewari,
Haryana, the driver of the bus stopped it at a Dhaba for breakfast on the service road side.

The mother of P1 was going to urinate towards footpath of service road and all of a sudden, the offending vehicle bearing No. HR-38S-4053 (Hayva) came from behind at a very high speed and hit the deceased, resulting in her falling down on the service road side and sustaining fatal injuries.
He deposed that the driver of the offending vehicle had ran away from the spot.
It is relevant to note here that the version as given in FIR, in the claim petition and in the testimony of PW1 are little different.

While according to the FIR lodged on the complaint of PW1, at the time of the accident, he alongwith deceased was going to a shop to have chai-pani (meal/beverages) when accident occurred on the service line, according to the claim petition, at the time of the accident, petitioner was standing on footpath at Dhaba side when she was hit by the offending vehicle and further, according to the testimony of PW1, at the time of accident, the deceased was going to urinate on footpath of the service road.

The site plan on record reflects the presence of some shops opposite to the place of accident at Point 'A' and site plan also shows that the accident took place on service road on the opposite side of shops.

The version in the FIR is first in point of time and shows that it was alleged in the complaint to the police that the deceased was going towards the shop for refreshment (chai-paani) at the time of accident.
However, according to the claim petition, she was standing on the footpath at Dhaba side.
However, both of these versions are contradicted in the testimony of petitioner, where he deposed that the deceased was going to urinate towards footpath of service road.
This seems to be the most correct version.
The site plan on record does not reflect that the petitioner was positioned towards Dhaba side and rather it suggests that she was in service lane right opposite to the shops and towards Nala side.

However, this contradiction regarding what witness was uphold at the time of accident and where she was exactly positioned on service road in itself is not material and does not throw away the case of the claimants.
Moving further, it is seen that during his cross-examination, PW1 deposed that he had seen the offending vehicle after the accident.
However, he denied that he did not witness the accident.
During his further cross-examination dt. 12.09.2023 as well
, PW1 admitted that he had seen the offending vehicle for the first time only after the accident.
However, this fact in itself does not in itself lead to the conclusion that PW1 had not at all witnessed the accident.
It is possible for an individual to observe an accident through his five senses including the sense of hearing and vision.

It is possible that while an individual may observe someone being hit with a forceful impact, he may observe the vehicle,
only after the collision has taken place and attention of that person might have been drawn or been on the victim first.

It cannot be lost sight of that petitioner denied that he was an eye-witness to the Abdul Kalam Etc vs Hamid Etc on 9 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/46110034/
4 accident.

sentences.text: It is not disputed that he was travelling with his mother on the date of accident and further that the bus in which they were traveling had taken a halt near the place of accident.
Testimony of PW1 suggests that petitioner had not observed the offending vehicle at the time of the same having hit against his mother.
There is likelihood of the same also in the wake of the fact that at the time of accident, deceased was going to ease herself on the roadside.
PW1 has not explained his position at the spot at the time of accident and even site plan does not reflect so.

Thus, it is quite possible that PW1 might not have actually witnessed the collusion of the offending vehicle against her mother and observed it for the first time only after the accident, despite being available near the spot.

However,
there is no denial of the fact that he was present at the spot and had seen the vehicle right after the accident.
Hence, he was at least a witness to res gestae and a fit witness to reflect on the circumstances at the spot.

FIR was registered on the same day without delay and in the FIR itself, it is mentioned that driver had fled away from the spot after leaving the offending truck and this in itself also points out towards the guilt of R1.

The road in question was a service lane and the offending vehicle was a transport vehicle in the category of Hevy Goods Vehicle (Open Body) and while plying the vehicle, it was the duty of the driver to take care of the pedestrians on the roadside.
The site plan reflects that the deceased was on the roadside/extreme corner at the time of accident.

Irrespective of the fact whether the deceased was present on the Dhaba side footpath or the other side of the road, it was the primary duty of R1 driving such a heavy vehicle to exercise due care and caution and the facts and circumstances of the case point out towards sheer negligence of R1.

In the written statement filed by R1 & R2, the very occurrence of accident has been denied and no such plea had been taken that the deceased was negligent in any manner or that she had suddenly come in front of the offending vehicle or that the accident could not be averted despite due care and precaution taken by R1.
A service lane refers to a road which provide access to properties or lane used for servicing vehicle.
It is a frontage road, which is usually a local road, running parallel to a higher speed, limited access road.

Duty of car of a driver of transport vehicle while driving in the service lane is to be more vigilant as the road is usually narrower and crowded in the case at hand, there were also shops on the road, indicative of the usual traffic on and around the road.
10. Respondent No.1 & Respondent No.2 i.e. Driver and Owner of the offending vehicle did not lead any evidence to prove anything contrary to the claim of the petitioner.

In the case of Cholamandalam MS General Insurance Company Ltd vs Smt. Kamlesh and Others2009 (3) AD Delhi 310 it was held that an adverse inference can be drawn when the driver of the offending vehicle does not enter into the witness box.

sentences.text: 11. After investigation, police filed the charge-sheet against respondent no. 1/Hamid, the driver of the offending car.
Filing of charge-sheet against the driver of offending vehicle prima-facie points to his culpability.
(New India Assurance Company Ltd vs Smt. Washeema Bano (2022) SCC OnLine All 403 and Mangla Ram vs Oriental Insurance Company Ltd (2018) 5SCC 656).

If the Tribunal feels that charge-sheet is collusive, it can record that charge-sheet cannot be accepted and call upon the parties at any stage to adduce oral evidence of accident and alleged negligence.
In such cases, issue of negligence must be decided on other evidence ignoring the charge-sheet.

13. Thus, in view of the above, this Tribunal is of the opinion that petitioners have been able to prove that there is sufficient material on record to establish that the accident had occurred due to rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle by respondent no.1 and that resulted into fatal injuries to the deceased victim Smt. Kosar.
Therefore, Issue No.1 is decided in favour of petitioners.
14. The onus to prove this issue was on Respondent No.3/Insurer but no evidence has been led by the insurance company on this issue.

IN case bearing citation "National Insurance Co. Ltd. Vs. Ram Pher", it has been held that insurance company has to establish any defence under Section 149(2) of MV Act so as to escape out from the liability on insurer to indemnify the insured.

entities.text: National Insurance Co. Ltd. Vs. Ram Pher
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Insurance Company has to plead and establish any fundamental breach of policy, terms and conditions in plying the vehicle on the road.
Copy of driving licence of R1 is on judicial record and reflects that the same was valid on the date of accident.
Accordingly, this issue is decided against R3/Insurer.

ISSUE No. 3.
15. Section 168 of the Act enjoins the Claims Tribunal to hold an inquiry into the claim to make an award determining the amount of compensation which appears to it to be just and reasonable.
The compensation should not be a windfall or a bonanza nor it should be pittance.
ASSESSMENT OF INCOME OF THE DECEASED:
16. PW1 is son of the deceased and one of the claimants.
It has come in his evidence that deceased was her mother aged 65 years 8 days and she was a house wife.
In proof of the economic status of deceased, PW1 had not filed on record any income and occupation proof of deceased.
Petitioners have not filed any documents in support of the educational qualification of the deceased.
No bank account statement of the deceased is filed either.
Further, it is seen that in the entire criminal case record, her address is mentioned as that of 10-B/167, Gali No.10, Chauhan Bangar, Jaffrabad, North East Delhi, 110053.
Her Aadhar Card as well as Adhar card of the petitioners show that the petitioners and deceased were residents of Delhi.
In the claim petition as well, address of the deceased is mentioned as that of Delhi.

In the absence of any income proof and education related proof of the deceased victim, her income has to be considered, being a resident of Delhi, as per the minimum wages applicable to an unskilled worker on the date of accident i.e. 09.01.2018.

Hence,
her income is considered to be Rs.13,818/- per month.

APPLICATION OF MULTIPLIER:
17.
The age of deceased was 65 years 8 days at the time of accident as per her Aadhar card Ex.PW1/3 shows her date of birth as 01.01.1953.
An appropriate multiplier has to be determined for computation of compensation.

The judgment titled as Sarla Verma v. DTC (2009) 6 SCC 121 is Abdul Kalam Etc vs Hamid Etc on 9 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/46110034/
6 relevant to consider the multiplier.

18.

Relevant parts of the judgment are reproduced here as under:
"(iii) While determining the income, an addition of 50% of actual salary to the income of the deceased towards future prospects, where the deceased had a permanent job and was below the age of 40 years, should be made.
The addition should be 30%, if the age of the deceased was between 40 to 50 years.

(iv) In case the deceased was self-employed or on a fixed salary, an addition of 40% of the established income should be the warrant where the deceased was below the age of 40 years.
An addition of 25% where the deceased was between the age of 40 to 50 years and 10% where the deceased was between the age of 50 to 60 years should be regarded as the necessary method of computation.
The established income means the income minus the tax component."
19. The deceased can be presumed to be as self-employed.
Since the deceased Kosar was 65 years, no future prospects shall be added to her income.
DEDUCTION TOWARDS PERSONAL LIVING EXPENSES:
20. After choosing the age, multiplier and income of the deceased, necessary deductions have to be made out of the income of the deceased towards her personal expenses.

Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Reshma Kumari & Ors. v. Madan Mohan & Anr., (2013) 9 SCC 65, in para 30, laid down the necessary deductions towards personal living and expenses of deceased as under :
Deductions out of earning of the Number of deceased dependents Married Persons Where dependent is 1 Half Where the number of dependent family 1/3rd members is 2 to 3 Where the number of dependent family 1/4th members is 4 to 6 Where the number of dependent family 1/5th members exceeds 6 (six) Deductions out of earning of the Number of deceased dependents Bachelor

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In case family is not large Half
In case dependents are the widowed 1/3rd mother and large number of younger non-earning sisters and brothers 21.
Petitioners are children of the deceased.
Petitioner Nos. 1 & Petitioner Nos. 5 to 9 are stated to be married children of the deceased and cannot be considered dependents of the deceased.
As per the memo of parties, Petitioner Nos. 2, 3 & 4 were unmarried on the date of accident and aged about 15 years, 13 years and 20 years on the date of filing of the claim petition in year 2018.

Ld. Counsel for petitioners submitted that though P4 was major and 20 years old on the date of accident, petitioner No. 4 was dependent on her mother on the date of accident and not working and thus, there are three dependents of the deceased.
Hence, only three petitioners i.e. Petitioner Nos.2 , 3 & 4 can be considered as dependent of the deceased being her children.
Hence, an amount of 1/3rd has to be deducted for personal and living expenses of the deceased.
22. Thus, the loss of dependency is computed as Rs.3,86,904/- (13,818 x 1/3 x 12 x 7).

23.

respectively has been fixed on account of loss of consortium, loss of estate and funeral expenses and Abdul Kalam Etc vs Hamid Etc on 9 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/46110034/

Further, in view of recent decision of Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case titled as United India Insurance Co. Ltd. Vs. Satinder Kaur @ Satwinder Kaur & Ors., Civil Appeal no. 2705 of 2020, decided on 30.06.2020, loss of consortium has to be fixed for each of the LRs.

(Rs.3,86,904/-+Rs.4,68,000/-) rounded off to Rs.8,55,000/- (Rupees Eight Lakhs Fifty Five Thousand only).

(ISSUE No.4) INTEREST :
24.
Petitioners shall also be entitled to interest @ 7.5% per annum on the award amount from the date of filing of the petition till its realization.
Thus, issue is accordingly decided in favour of the petitioners and against the respondents.

LIABILITY:
25.
Now, the question arises as to which of the respondents are liable to pay the compensation amount.
As the vehicle was insured with IFFCO Tokio General Insurance Company Ltd. on the date of accident, it is clear that R3/Insurer is liable to compensate the petitioners.

sentences.text: No evidence has been led by the insurance company to establish that any terms and conditions of the insurance policy was breached by the insured.
Thus, the Respondent No.3, being insurer of the offending vehicle, is liable to pay the compensation amount to the petitioners.

ISSUE No. 5/ RELIEF:
26.

In view of the findings on said issues, this Tribunal awards a total compensation of Rs.8,55,000/- (Rupees Eight Lakhs Fifty Five Thousand only) alongwith interest @ 7.5% per annum on the aforesaid award amount from the date of filing of the petition till realization in favour of petitioners and against the respondent no.3 /IFFCO Tokio General Insurance Company.
This award is required to be deposited with this Tribunal within 30 days.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
8. In an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and in fact, is the preponderance of probabilities which is applied in civil cases.
It is also the law that the tribunal is not bound by the technical rules of evidence.
It is possible that while an individual may observe someone being hit with a forceful impact, he may observe the vehicle,
only after the collision has taken place and attention of that person might have been drawn or been on the victim first.
The road in question was a service lane and the offending vehicle was a transport vehicle in the category of Hevy Goods Vehicle (Open Body) and while plying the vehicle, it was the duty of the driver to take care of the pedestrians on the roadside.
Irrespective of the fact whether the deceased was present on the Dhaba side footpath or the other side of the road, it was the primary duty of R1 driving such a heavy vehicle to exercise due care and caution and the facts and circumstances of the case point out towards sheer negligence of R1.
In the case of Cholamandalam MS General Insurance Company Ltd vs Smt. Kamlesh and Others2009 (3) AD Delhi 310 it was held that an adverse inference can be drawn when the driver of the offending vehicle does not enter into the witness box.
(New India Assurance Company Ltd vs Smt. Washeema Bano (2022) SCC OnLine All 403 and Mangla Ram vs Oriental Insurance Company Ltd (2018) 5SCC 656).
12. In New India Assurance Company Ltd vs Pazhaniammal (2011) (2) KLT 648, the Hon'ble High Court of Kerala has held that as a general rule, it can be accepted that production of charge-sheet is prima-facie sufficient evidence of negligence for the purpose of claim under section 166 MV Act.
any party does not accept such charge-sheet, the burden must be on such party to adduce evidence.
If the Tribunal feels that charge-sheet is collusive, it can record that charge-sheet cannot be accepted and call upon the parties at any stage to adduce oral evidence of accident and alleged negligence.
In such cases, issue of negligence must be decided on other evidence ignoring the charge-sheet.
The compensation should not be a windfall or a bonanza nor it should be pittance.

16. PW1 is son of the deceased and one of the claimants.
It has come in his evidence that deceased was her mother aged 65 years 8 days and she was a house wife.
In proof of the economic status of deceased, PW1 had not filed on record any income and occupation proof of deceased.
Petitioners have not filed any documents in support of the educational qualification of the deceased.
No bank account statement of the deceased is filed either.
In the absence of any income proof and education related proof of the deceased victim, her income has to be considered, being a resident of Delhi, as per the minimum wages applicable to an unskilled worker on the date of accident i.e. 09.01.2018.

6 relevant to consider the multiplier.
20. After choosing the age, multiplier and income of the deceased, necessary deductions have to be made out of the income of the deceased towards her personal expenses.
Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Reshma Kumari & Ors. v. Madan Mohan & Anr., (2013) 9 SCC 65, in para 30, laid down the necessary deductions towards personal living and expenses of deceased as under :
